curriculum.title: Strings, Quotes and Length
curriculum.answer:
## Strings, quotes and length

Text in Python is called a string, meaning a sequence of characters such as a word or sentence. A string is written with matching single quotes or double quotes around the characters. Both styles make the same kind of value, so you can choose the style that keeps your sentence readable.

```python
a = 'Paris'
b = "rabbit"
print(a)
print(b)
```
```text
Paris
rabbit
```

The examples show the origin of every value: `a` and `b` are created first, then printed. Quoted digits are still strings. `'1975'` is text, not a number, so `+` will glue it rather than do arithmetic.

Use `+` to concatenate strings, meaning glue the right part after the left part. Use `*` with a number to repeat a string. Use `len()` to count characters, including spaces and punctuation. It counts characters in the resulting string value; the surrounding source-code quote marks are not counted.

```python
first = 'Good'
second = 'night'
full = first + ' ' + second
print(full)
print(len(full))
print(3 * 'un' + 'ium')
```
```text
Good night
10
unununium
```

Here `first` and `second` are created by the assignments at the start of this standalone example. In the coding task, input names are supplied separately by the checker. `full` is built only from those inputs plus one literal space. Its length is 10 because `len()` counts 4 letters, 1 space, and 5 letters. A common mistake is writing `first + second` and losing the space, or writing `'1975' + '75'` and expecting `2050`. Another mistake is mixing text and numbers, as in `'yum' + 5`, which raises `TypeError` because both sides of string `+` must be strings.
